coherence.reasons: Both run the same market, economics, cash, alternative sequence, with titles that state conclusions and an executive summary that mirrors the sections. X adds an explicit six-condition test of the founders' hypothesis (slide 3) that maps one-to-one onto the sections, so every later slide answers a named condition, and its options table and cash model tie back to the governing thought. Y is tidy and consistent, but its Zipcart material is split across the market and unit-economics sections, and its reopening conditions connect less tightly to the analysis ("rider pay rules are settled" is not derived from any threshold). X has one internal blemish: the sensitivity chart on slide 7 has three labels shifted (riders, density and promotions values are swapped), though the title and text conclusions are correct.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: decline the launch, fund software and package fast delivery for grocers. X weighs alternatives more fully. It models a one-store pilot and rejects it with reasons (loses money at median, breaches runway in month 10, little new learning), and it rejects extending the pop-up. It stress-tests its own recommendation by finding the 34% ARR growth floor and phasing hires against signed contracts, with a 90-day checkpoint. Its re-entry triggers are quantified (AOV at least $42, 3.0 orders per rider-hour, about 1,050 orders a day, or a fee losing no more than 15% of volume). Y compares only launch versus software, never considers a capped test, asserts rather than tests that the software path keeps runway, and its reopening conditions are vaguer.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core figures right: −$6.17 at median, −$1.76 at best observed, −$12.57 for the pop-up, +$2.02 on plan, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, −$18.2M for nine stores, and −$1.05 for Zipcart's moves on a median store. X goes further on the critical evidence. It states the 41.5% CAGR, gives break-even AOVs for every scenario, and computes the roughly 1,042 orders a day needed with Zipcart's fee, conceding that a profitable route may exist at high density. It also quantifies the rider-pay risk (+$1.48 per order), runs a one-driver-at-median sensitivity on the plan, sanity-checks the plan's implied $266M of sales against QuickBasket's revenue, and models both readings of the $9.5M month by month. Its ambiguities are disclosed in an appendix. X's one error is the mislabelled bars on slide 7, which does not change its stated conclusions. Y's numbers are clean, including a correct step-by-step bridge from −$6.17 to +$2.02 and a sound 27.6-month payback. But Y uses the Zipcart evidence only to dismiss it ("pricing, not better operations"), without testing what density would make the fee work, and it says less about the pop-up growth caveat.

revision.reasons: Both correctly reject the founders' hypothesis while granting that market growth is real. X handles it more explicitly: it restates the hypothesis, breaks it into six conditions that would have to be true, and tests each. It addresses the founders' capability claim directly (the pop-up ran below median on all four drivers) and gives the fair caveat that the pop-up was early, then shows ramp-up to median still loses $6.17. It also engages with the partly supportive Zipcart evidence rather than only dismissing it, and turns it into a re-entry trigger. Y concedes demand, notes the Midwest claim is untestable from the pack, and observes that running the 14 sites has not made them profitable. But it treats the Zipcart case as pure rebuttal and does not ask under what conditions the founders could be right.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with correct core numbers. X serves the board better because it pre-empts the likely counter-proposals (a single pilot store, extending the pop-up, copying Zipcart's fee) and shows quantitatively why each fails. It also tests the recommended software path against the runway rule and finds the growth floor at which it breaks, and it gives measurable re-entry triggers and a 90-day checkpoint. Y is shorter and clean, with a good payback calculation and input bridge, but it leaves the pilot option and the conditions under which a fee could work unaddressed, and its software runway claim is asserted more than shown. X's chart-label slip is minor against that extra decision value.
